evals.prompt: I help run the Leeds Elixir meetup - three years running, we consistently get 130-140 people at the monthly sessions and there are about 900 people in the Slack. A friend who organizes events told me the rule of thumb is once you pass 500 community members you should launch a conference, so we're planning ElixirNorth as a two-day conference next autumn. There are four of us organizing, all with day jobs, and we've never run a CFP before. Can you help us figure out the right setup?
evals.expected_output: A format brief that rejects the headcount rule of thumb, recommends a single-day single-track conference as the graduation target instead of a two-day debut, gates the jump on content depth and venue-risk tolerance, and validates section by section after an interview.
expectations: Recommends a single-day, single-track conference as the graduation target rather than endorsing the two-day conference plan
Rejects the 500-community-member rule of thumb, and any fixed headcount, as the graduation gate
States the published graduation trigger: a meetup consistently at 100-150+, enough quality local speakers for one curated day, and a team willing to carry venue risk
Cites divergent debut sizes (DartUP jumping at around 250, GopherCon debuting at 700) as evidence that no fixed headcount gates the jump
Flags the never-run-a-CFP fact as the open content-supply question, since content depth and speaker supply gate the jump
Cites North Bay Python's inaugural benchmark: roughly a $40,000 budget, planned in under 6 months
Gates any multi-day option on content depth and travel justification, citing Strange Loop's benchmark that 2-3 days is the sweet spot and 1-day conferences are not worth the travel time
Keeps the recurring meetup running as the demand engine for the conference rather than replacing it
Asks interview questions before recommending a structure, including at least the effort ceiling for four organizers with day jobs and whether this is a one-off bet or a compounding annual asset
Presents 2-3 candidate structures with trade-offs and one explicit recommendation
Proposes validating the structure section by section with explicit user approval rather than delivering one final block
Points first-edition sizing and launch logistics to a dedicated first-edition process rather than covering launch planning inline

evals.prompt: PulseConf is our single-track TypeScript conference, 300 attendees, third edition coming up. This year's CFP pulled 105 submissions for 22 slots and rejecting that many great talks feels wasteful - honestly it makes me think our CFP process is broken. The plan for next year is to split into a frontend track and a backend track so we can accept twice as much. Sanity-check this before we announce it?
evals.expected_output: A recommendation to stay single track: the roughly 4.8x oversubscription sits well below the published 8-10x multi-track trigger, high rejection rates are normal at popular single-track events, and the rejected content gets an outlet through an open-space afternoon or ignite block instead of a second track.
expectations: Recommends keeping the single track and advises against adding the second track next year
Computes or states the oversubscription ratio from the given figures (roughly 4.8x, about 5x)
States the published multi-track promotion condition: a CFP pool oversubscribed roughly 8-10x beyond slots
Cites the benchmark of 8-12 speakers per day per track, or the 200-1,200 applicant pool range for a JSConf-tier event
States that 8-30x oversubscription is normal at a popular single-track conference and rejects the user's conclusion that the CFP process is broken
Frames multi-track as a scale and attendee-agency decision, never a quality upgrade
Cites the independent single-track convergence of named events, naming at least two of Strange Loop, GOTO, Monktoberfest, Deconstruct, SmashingConf
Names what multi-track sells off: the shared experience or story arc and the organizer's editorial control
Offers an outlet for content that misses the curated track, such as an open-space afternoon or an ignite block
States that if multi-track is ever adopted, plenary moments (opening keynote, shared lunch, closing) must be added to preserve shared experience
States that track count and content-mix policy are one coupled decision, not two separate ones
Records the revision trigger for next edition: re-read CFP pressure against the roughly 8-10x floor, treating that floor as where the conversation opens rather than an automatic switch

evals.prompt: I run developer marketing at NimbusWorks and own our annual user conference - about 400 attendees. Our VP wants next year's edition to be hybrid: 'best of both worlds, more reach, and low risk since we keep the in-person part anyway.' In the post-event survey a bunch of people did ask for a livestream. Budget is flat year over year. What do we need to plan to make hybrid work?
evals.expected_output: A pushback on the premise: interactive hybrid is the maximum-cost, maximum-risk option, backed by the published CHI finances, with in-person plus record-and-post recommended instead and a concrete promotion condition under which hybrid would be revisited.
expectations: Advises against interactive hybrid rather than answering the how-to question as asked
Rejects the 'low risk / best of both worlds' framing explicitly: hybrid is the maximum-cost, maximum-risk option, two simultaneous productions, not a middle ground
Cites the published cost evidence that hybrid roughly doubles AV and logistics cost
Cites CHI 2022's loss of $484,886 (or approximately $485K) as the published cautionary figure
States that low virtual registration fees did not cover the cost of virtual inclusion and were subsidized by in-person fees
Treats the survey requests for a livestream as non-evidence of paying remote demand
Cites the figure that free livestreams draw well under 10% of sign-ups
Flags that the sub-10% livestream figure comes from academic conferencing, not tech, and is indicative only
Recommends in-person with talks recorded and posted afterward (or a one-feed unmonitored stream) as the default delivery mode
States the hybrid promotion condition: remote registrations reliably above roughly 25-30% of paid attendance and covering their marginal cost
Names the flat budget as directly contradicting the dedicated production budget hybrid requires, sized for roughly double AV and logistics
Sets a next-edition measurement: compare engaged remote attendance against the published benchmarks before the hybrid question is reopened

evals.prompt: We're organizing CodeSprint, a 48-hour student hackathon at the university in March - expecting around 250 hackers, about 40 teams. Since some teams are remote we planned it hybrid: on-site at the engineering building plus a Discord server for the remote teams, and everyone gets judged together at the end. For judging we're leaning toward having every team pitch on stage to the jury. Does this hold up?
evals.expected_output: A refusal of the hybrid hackathon plan - pick in-person or fully digital and commit - backed by MLH's position and named failure modes, plus a judging structure that scales to 40 teams: expo tables by default, two-stage only if a legible finale is needed.
expectations: Refuses the hybrid hackathon plan and recommends committing to either in-person or fully digital
States that for hackathons hybrid is deleted outright, not merely deprioritized or made conditional
Cites MLH's refusal of hybrid hackathons as worse for both organizers and hackers

Names at least two concrete hybrid-hackathon failure modes, such as remote attendees feeling second-class, inconsistent judging when remote teams cannot present science-fair style, sponsor interactions skewing to the booth, or swag and prize fulfilment skewing in-person
States that a well-run digital hackathon is more than just a Discord server, so the planned Discord layer does not make the event digital-capable
Advises against having all 40 teams pitch on stage because serial stage pitching does not scale
Recommends expo-table (science-fair style) judging as the default because judges rotate in parallel and it scales
Offers two-stage expo-then-finals as the structure to use when press or sponsor reporting needs a legible on-stage finale
Notes video-only judging as the digital-format default and the only structure that scales past what judge-hours allow
Matches demo format to jury composition: technical judges need to touch the demo, business judges need the narrative slot
Hands the scoring rubric, weights, and jury mechanics to a separate judging process rather than designing them here
Presents fully digital as a legitimate deliberate choice if the remote teams matter, not as a downgrade from in-person

evals.prompt: First edition of HelmForge Day, a community DevOps conference - single day, 220 registered so far, and money is tight. Our platinum sponsor just offered to double their contribution if their CTO can host a panel on stage with two of their customers, and they floated a 'sponsored keynote' too. Separately I was thinking a panel of local engineering leaders would be an easy way to fill the dead 4pm slot. How should we play this?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to sell any program slot, a counter-offer built from legitimate sponsor inventory, and both panels cut: panels are deleted from a first event, with a fireside chat or one more curated talk in the 4pm slot instead.
expectations: Refuses to sell the panel or sponsored keynote to the sponsor - no sponsor buys a program slot
States the community-event sponsor inventory: expo, side events, and 1-minute inter-talk slots, never the stage

Cites at least one named precedent for refusing sold program content, such as Strange Loop never selling keynotes, CNCF's no-sales-pitch wording, or DevOpsDays' rule that no sponsor may buy a speaking slot
Deletes panels from this first event entirely rather than demoting or conditionally allowing them
Cites at least one named panel critic among Fred Wilson, Brad Feld, Scott Berkun, and Duncan Green
Names a structural panel flaw, such as four panelists' 5-minute introductions burning 20 minutes, or the moderator being too deferential to challenge guests
Rejects the fill-the-4pm-slot reasoning as the known failure mode of scheduling a panel to flatter sponsors or fill a gap
Offers the substitution for the 4pm slot: a fireside chat or one more curated talk
States the panel promotion condition reserved for established events: a strong, prepared, willing-to-interrupt moderator with pre-briefed provocative questions and no long self-introductions
Explains the neutrality rationale: credibility and attendee trust come from refusing sold stage content
Routes the funding gap to the event's budget and funding structure rather than solving it with program inventory
Makes a concrete counter-offer to the platinum sponsor from legitimate inventory, such as expo presence, a side event, or a 1-minute inter-talk slot

evals.prompt: Help me design the day for KernelDay: one day, single room, about 200 attendees, community-run. Current draft is 45-minute talks back to back from 9 to 6 with 10-minute breaks. Two goals this year: get more first-time speakers on stage, and lean into the fact that attendees keep telling us the best part is the conversations between sessions. One headache: the CFP attracted a pile of vendor tool-demo submissions we don't want on the main stage but hate to just reject.
evals.expected_output: A day architecture built from the session-format catalog: shorter curated talks in the morning, an ignite block for first-time speakers, an open-space afternoon absorbing the vendor tool content, and the hallway track protected as a designed choice with long breaks.
expectations: Shortens the curated talks from 45 minutes to roughly 25-30 minutes, citing that length as a sourced balance point for content rather than an arbitrary preference
Adds an ignite block as the format that gets first-time speakers on stage at lower commitment
States the ignite mechanics: 5 minutes, 20 slides, auto-advancing on a fixed timer
States that the auto-advance mechanic, not organizer discipline, is what enforces the length
Includes ignite operational safeguards: collect slides in advance and run the whole block from one dedicated laptop, never presenters' own machines
Steers the vendor tool-demo submissions to open space instead of the curated stage, as the content-mix rule
States that the single track is what makes the tool-talks-to-open-space rule enforceable - track count and content policy are one coupled decision
Proposes a day shape with curated talks in the morning, an ignite block, and open space in the afternoon
Describes real open-space ceremony elements, such as the marketplace or agenda wall, facilitators handling logistics but never content, or the Law of Two Feet
Treats the hallway track as a designed format choice: lengthens breaks or otherwise protects unstructured time instead of keeping the packed 9-to-6 grid
Cites Monktoberfest as the precedent for optimizing structure around the hallway track, such as its late start time
Keeps an explicit written ban on sales pitches from the curated track
Picks session-mix measurement signals with revision triggers written down before the event, such as the open-space wall filling or ignite application volume

evals.prompt: GreenStack Conf has sold out two editions at 450 people, and next year we're expanding from one day to three. What percentage of a conference should be workshops? I read somewhere the industry standard is around 30% hands-on content. We were also thinking of running the workshops in parallel with the talks so attendees can pick their own mix.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to endorse any industry-average workshop percentage, per-event named ratios cited instead, and the bracketing model recommended: optional separately ticketed workshop days around the talk days rather than workshops running parallel to the curated track.
expectations: Refuses to give an industry-average workshop percentage and declines the 30% figure rather than adjusting it

Cites named per-event ratios instead, naming at least two of: SmashingConf's 2 workshop days plus 2 conference days, PyCon's separately paid tutorial days, GOTO's masterclass day, DevOpsDays' optional pre-event workshop day
States the rule explicitly: report workshop ratios as named-event examples and never collapse them into one industry number
Recommends the bracketing model: optional workshop days placed before or after the talk days
States that workshop days under the bracketing model are separately ticketed
Advises against running workshops in parallel with the curated talks because it dilutes the curated track
Names the separately ticketed workshop day as a real revenue lever
Checks the one-day-to-three-day jump against content depth and travel justification rather than the sellouts alone, citing the 2-3-day sweet-spot benchmark
Explains that the workshop day stops competing for program hours once it moves out of the program into its own ticketed day
Sets workshop sell-through measurement with a threshold fixed in advance, such as 60% of capacity, with fewer workshop days next edition if missed
States that the bracketing model makes the workshop-day decision reversible edition to edition
Hands workshop-day execution - capacity, facilitators, prerequisites, environment setup - to a dedicated workshop process rather than designing it here

evals.prompt: I organize DataForge Summit, our company's annual user conference - around 350 attendees. The audience is split roughly half data-platform engineers, half analytics managers and directors. The feedback is contradictory every year: engineers say the talks are too fluffy, managers say they're too deep. Our fix for next year is to brief every speaker to pitch their talk at an intermediate level so it works for everyone. Good plan?
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the flat intermediate difficulty band, replaced by the two-audience track split: two tracks under one banner keyed to depth, with per-session maturity tags, preserved plenary moments, and the vendor-conference pole named where it changes the defaults.
expectations: Rejects briefing every speaker to an intermediate level - a flat difficulty band serves neither audience
Applies the two-audience promotion condition: two genuinely different audiences sharing the same underlying problem at different depths justify two tracks under one banner
Distinguishes this condition from the CFP-oversubscription trigger, noting it is a separate promotion path
Recommends tagging each session with a maturity or depth level so each track carries sessions at the depth its audience wants
Structures the split by depth and audience - decision-makers wanting the why, practitioners wanting the how - rather than by technology topic alone
Preserves plenary moments such as an opening keynote, shared lunch, or closing alongside the track split
Identifies the event as the vendor/user-conference pole and says which recommendations assume which pole
Notes that vendor conferences run invited content organized around the vendor's architecture with a narrower vertical scope
Does not frame the second track as a quality upgrade - frames it as an audience and agency decision
Keeps the two tracks under one event banner rather than proposing two separate events
Records the revision trigger for next edition, such as per-track attendance or depth feedback deciding whether the split stays
Asks for audience evidence or interview answers, such as numbers behind the audience split, before finalizing the structure
